strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: virtual screening over ultra-large combinatorial synthesis libraries (CSLs), where exhaustive docking is infeasible.

The APEX factorization is a clever engineering contribution that exploits CSL hierarchy to amortize surrogate evaluation, enabling scoring of a 10B-compound library in tens of seconds on a single T4 GPU.

Provides a large benchmark resource: a fully enumerated 12M-compound CSL with docking scores for five targets and physicochemical properties, enabling ground-truth top-k evaluation and constraint testing.
The paper is generally well written and clearly organized, with informative figures and a detailed appendix on the GPU top-k implementation.
Evaluation includes multiple targets, several drug-likeness constraint sets, and a comparison to Thompson sampling, showing APEX is competitive under matched budgets in some settings.
weaknesses: Constraint handling is weaker than claimed: Figure 3B indicates that for stringent constraints (e.g., Astex Rule of 3) only about 30% of APEX-retrieved compounds actually satisfy the constraints, and for Lipinski/Pfizer the rate is around 80–85%. This substantially undercuts the claim that APEX 'effectively satisfies diverse constraint sets' and is not accompanied by precision/false-positive analysis or a strategy for exact post-filtering.

Ranking accuracy at larger k is modest: Figure 3A shows that with k=100,000, recall of the true top-100,000 is only about 0.2 for unconstrained PARP1 and lower for several constrained settings, meaning roughly 80% of the true top-100k are missed. The paper does not report recall for larger k despite APEX's exhaustive-search capability, nor does it compare to strong hierarchical/virtual-screening baselines such as V-SYNTHES.

No ground-truth validation on the 10B library: only runtime and CDF enrichment are shown. It is therefore unclear whether APEX retrieves high-scoring compounds in the ultra-large setting, which is the central claimed advantage.

The theoretical discussion is thin: the claim that noise injection into embeddings makes the factorized APEX prediction robust to errors-in-variables is hand-wavy, with no formal error analysis, bound on factorization error, or guarantee relating surrogate/factorization error to top-k recall.

The benchmark CSL is constructed via BRICS fragmentation of ZINC22 and is explicitly not guaranteed to be synthetically feasible. This limits relevance to real make-on-demand CSLs, and performance on actual libraries such as Enamine REAL is unknown.

Reproducibility is limited: there is no code or data availability statement, docking relies on a custom GPU AutoDock Vina implementation, and key details (number of factorizer training samples, coverage of unseen synthons/reactions, hyperparameters, training times) are not reported.

The data split is not fully clarified: the surrogate is trained on a 1M compound CSL and evaluated on 12M/10B CSLs, but it is unclear whether the 1M library is disjoint from the 12M library or whether overlapping compounds could inflate recall.

The paper lacks a limitations section: failure modes for non-additive properties, unseen reactions/synthons, and constraint-prediction errors are not discussed, nor are broader ethical/dual-use considerations.

strengths: Targets an important and timely problem: exhaustive virtual screening over ultra-large combinatorial synthesis libraries (CSLs) under limited scoring budgets.

The APEX factorization is technically well-motivated: by training a surrogate with linear task heads and factorizing its embeddings into synthon/R-group contributions, it enables exhaustive approximate scoring without O(|X_D|) neural network evaluations.

The GPU top-k implementation is a substantial engineering contribution, achieving end-to-end retrieval of k=1,000,000 from a 10B compound CSL in ~21–24 seconds on a single T4 GPU, with an order-of-magnitude speedup over the CPU implementation.

The paper constructs a large benchmark CSL (12M fully enumerated compounds) with docking scores on five targets and RDKit physicochemical properties, which could be a valuable resource for evaluating virtual screening algorithms if released.

The method handles user-specified constraints declaratively via a lexicographic priority queue, and Figure 3B shows that retrieved sets satisfy constraints at rates above the library baseline for several constraint sets.
The comparison with Thompson sampling, while limited, shows APEX often outperforms or matches TS at matched evaluation budgets, especially at lower budgets.
The limitations section acknowledges that the benchmark does not ensure synthetic feasibility, which is an honest caveat.
weaknesses: The empirical comparison is insufficient to support the central claim of 'consistently strong performance ... compared to alternative methods.' The only baseline is Thompson sampling, evaluated on the top five largest reactions and only in the unconstrained setting. No comparison is made to V-SYNTHES or other synthon-based CSL screening methods, despite V-SYNTHES being cited as a primary alternative.

The paper does not disentangle surrogate model error from factorizer approximation error. It evaluates APEX against docking ground truth but never reports how the factorized predictions compare to the original surrogate predictions on the same 12M library. Thus it is unclear whether the observed recall is due to a good surrogate or a good factorization; the appendix R² values are not discussed in the main text.

There is no ground-truth top-k evaluation on the 10B compound library. The 10B experiment only reports runtime and enrichment against the 12M background distribution, which does not validate retrieval accuracy on the ultra-large library that is the paper's main target.

Reproducibility is severely limited: the paper does not provide code, model weights, or the generated benchmark library, and it omits key training details such as architecture, hyperparameters, data splits, random seeds, and how the factorizer is trained on 10B compounds without labels.

Potential data leakage/overlap is not adequately addressed. The surrogate is trained on a 1M compound CSL and evaluated on 12M/10B CSLs, but the paper does not state whether these sets are disjoint; if the 1M set is a subset or overlaps with the evaluation libraries, reported recall may be inflated.

The benchmark CSL is not a real combinatorial synthesis library: it is built by BRICS fragmentation and recombination of ZINC22 compounds without synthetic feasibility. This limits the practical significance for real virtual screening campaigns on libraries like Enamine REAL.

Constraint satisfaction is only approximate. Figure 3B shows that for stringent sets like Astex Rule of 3 the top-k satisfaction rate is low (around 0.3), meaning many retrieved compounds still violate true constraints; the paper does not analyze false-positive/negative constraint predictions or the impact of true violations on downstream screening.

The theoretical runtime example (evaluating one trillion compounds in 'just a few seconds') is not consistent with the reported actual runtime (~21 seconds for 10B compounds, which would scale to much longer for 1T). Overheads in top-k retrieval dominate, so the example overstates the practical scaling.
The paper calls the T4 GPU a 'consumer GPU' in the abstract, but the T4 is a datacenter GPU; this is a minor but misleading characterization.

The method is purely greedy on surrogate predictions and lacks any uncertainty quantification or exploration mechanism. This may miss high-scoring compounds when the surrogate is uncertain, yet the paper does not evaluate this failure mode.
No ablations are provided for key design choices, including embedding dimension d=64, the noise-injection training scheme, the factorization architecture, and the linear task-head assumption.

strengths: Enables exhaustive surrogate-based screening of ultra-large CSLs (10B compounds) in under 30 seconds on a single T4 GPU by caching synthon associative contributions and using a GPU top-k algorithm.
Provides a new benchmark CSL with over 12M fully enumerated compounds annotated with docking scores on five targets and physicochemical properties, enabling ground-truth top-k evaluation.
Demonstrates strong recall relative to random baselines and competitive performance versus Thompson sampling, especially at low evaluation budgets.
Clearly describes the hierarchical factorization and GPU implementation, and the use of noise during surrogate training is a reasonable attempt to mitigate errors-in-variables.
Addresses a practical need for declarative queries with constraints in virtual screening and shows useful runtime scaling to ultra-large libraries.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is limited: no code or data availability statement, no training details (training time, hardware, hyperparameters, data splits), and no release of the benchmark CSL or docking scores.

The comparison to Thompson sampling is not apples-to-apples: APEX uses a pre-trained surrogate and cheaply evaluates all compounds, while TS uses expensive docking evaluations; matching k to total TS evaluations conflates retrieval budget with oracle evaluation budget.

No ablation isolates factorization error from surrogate error: since the 12M library is fully enumerated, the authors could compare top-k recall using the original surrogate versus the factorized surrogate, but they do not.

Constraint handling is weak for stringent constraint sets: for Astex Rule of 3, only about 30% of retrieved top-k compounds satisfy true constraints, and top-100 recall is as low as 0.17 on PARP1, despite the lexicographic priority queue intended to enforce constraints.
The theoretical justification for noise injection (errors-in-variables) is hand-wavy; no formal or empirical analysis quantifies how factorization error affects ranking.
The CSL is built via BRICS fragmentation without ensuring synthetic feasibility, so it may not reflect real make-on-demand libraries, limiting practical significance.
No comparison to other virtual screening methods (e.g., V-SYNTHES, NGT) beyond Thompson sampling.
Training cost and data requirements (1M labeled compounds) are not discussed; for a new target, the surrogate and factorizer must be retrained, which may be expensive.
No dedicated limitations section; broader impacts and potential dual-use are not addressed.

strengths: Proposes an original factorization-based surrogate for combinatorial synthesis libraries (CSLs): APEX decomposes molecular embedding predictions into cached per-synthon associative contributions, enabling exhaustive approximate top-k search over libraries with billions to tens of billions of compounds on a single GPU.

Demonstrates strong practical utility and runtime: APEX can retrieve top-1M compounds from a 10B CSL in roughly 30 seconds on a T4 GPU under drug-likeness constraints, and can be applied zero-shot to the 70B Enamine REAL library with docking-score enrichment over background distributions.

Provides a useful benchmark: a fully enumerated 12M-compound CSL annotated with docking scores for five diverse targets and many physicochemical properties, enabling ground-truth top-j evaluation and comparison of virtual screening algorithms.

Evaluation includes multiple relevant dimensions: top-j recall at matched budgets, constraint satisfaction rates, comparison to Thompson sampling on selected reactions, zero-shot transfer to Enamine REAL, and an error decomposition separating surrogate and factorizer errors.

Method is well-motivated and clearly positioned relative to surrogate-based, generative, synthon-based, and dense-retrieval virtual screening approaches; the factorization strategy is complementary to existing molecular encoders and amortizes across repeated declarative queries.
The paper is generally well-organized, with a clear three-step APEX protocol and detailed appendix descriptions of architectures, training, constraint sets, and GPU top-k implementation.
weaknesses: The central claim of consistently strong performance versus alternative methods is not fully supported by the experiments. The only algorithmic comparison is to Thompson sampling, and that comparison is limited to the five largest reactions, unconstrained objectives, and matched evaluation budgets; other virtual screening and active-learning baselines are not evaluated.

Retrieval accuracy is moderate rather than uniformly strong. For example, unconstrained top-100 recall ranges roughly from 0.38 to 0.78 across targets, constrained recall is often around 0.2–0.45, and top-100k recall is often near 0.2; the paper’s framing as “exact retrieval” and “exhaustive” should be more carefully qualified as approximate under the factorized surrogate.

Potential data leakage is not adequately resolved. The surrogate is trained on a 1M-compound CSL and evaluated on a 12M-compound CSL, but both are downsampled from the same 10B CSL and it is unclear whether they are disjoint. If the 1M training set overlaps the 12M evaluation set, top-j recall may be inflated.

The main quantitative benchmark is built by BRICS fragmentation of ZINC22 lead-like molecules without ensuring synthetic feasibility. This makes it a CSL-like benchmark rather than a true make-on-demand CSL, so the primary results may not fully reflect real combinatorial synthesis libraries. The Enamine REAL experiment is zero-shot and lacks ground-truth top-k labels, so it provides enrichment evidence but not retrieval accuracy.

The factorized model is additive over R-group assignments and does not explicitly represent pairwise or higher-order epistasis between different R-groups. For docking or binding objectives with strong fragment interactions, this expressiveness limitation could materially reduce recall; the paper does not analyze or ablate this issue.

The theoretical justification for noise injection in the surrogate embeddings is informal. The claim that adding isotropic noise regularizes against an errors-in-variables problem is not supported by a formal guarantee, a controlled ablation, or a quantitative robustness analysis.

Surrogate prediction accuracy is not reported in the main text; the appendix figure is not summarized with R-squared or correlation values. This makes it difficult to judge whether recall is limited primarily by the surrogate, the factorizer, or the top-k search procedure.

Reproducibility is weakened by the absence of an explicit code or data repository link in the manuscript, despite references to a code repository and an “open” CSL. Data availability, preprocessing time, and the separation between one-time training costs and amortized search runtime are not fully detailed.

There is no dedicated limitations section. Some limitations are noted in passing, such as lack of synthetic feasibility and reduced zero-shot enrichment, but they are not systematically discussed or stress-tested.

strengths: Targets an important and timely problem: efficient top-k retrieval with constraints over ultra-large combinatorial synthesis libraries (CSLs), which is a genuine bottleneck for virtual screening at 10^10+ scale.

The core factorization idea (decomposing the surrogate embedding into cached per-synthon associative contributions, Eq. 9-17) enables amortized exhaustive scoring, and the demonstrated scaling (10B BRICS and 70B Enamine REAL in ~11-200s on a single T4, Table 1) is a non-trivial engineering achievement.

Contributes a reusable benchmark: a 12M-compound CSL fully enumerated with ground-truth docking scores on five diverse targets plus RDKit properties, enabling direct ground-truth top-k evaluation (Section 3, Section 5.1).

The error decomposition (Appendix A.6, Eq. 24-25, Figure 8) separating surrogate, factorizer, and cross-term error is a genuinely useful diagnostic and the empirical finding that the cross term is negligible is informative.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported: a code repository is referenced, and architectures, dimensions, parameter counts, optimizer and training details are given (Appendix A.8).
The zero-shot application to Enamine REAL (Section 5.3.1) is a useful generality check beyond the self-built library.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the factorizer (SynthonEncoder/RgroupEncoder/ReactionEncoder plus value/key associative decomposition, Eq. 6-12) is directly adapted from Pedawi et al. (2022); the contribution is repurposing it to reconstruct surrogate embeddings rather than a generative decoder. The paper acknowledges this dependence but still claims firstness for a narrow combination.

Evaluation rests on a single baseline (Thompson sampling, Section 5.2) that is run only in the unconstrained setting, only on the five largest reactions (~4M of the 12M library), and which the authors themselves note is limited (per-reaction bandits). No comparison is made to Deep Docking, MolPal, MEMES, active learning, or even a plain exhaustive-surrogate baseline to isolate the factorizer's effect on top-k recall.

The central claim of 'consistently strong performance compared to alternative methods' is oversold relative to the evidence: recall of the ground-truth top-100 at k=100,000 is only roughly 0.4-0.8, and top-100,000 recall is ~0.2 (Figure 2A). Large fractions of the true top-j set are missed, so the abstract's 'exact retrieval of approximate top-k sets' is technically true but practically weak.

Possible train/eval overlap: the surrogate is trained on the 1M CSL and evaluated on the 12M/10B CSLs (Section 4 end, Section 5), but the smaller libraries are described as uniform downsamples of the same reactions (Section 3.1), so the training set may be largely contained in the evaluation set. The paper asserts this 'addresses data leakage' without establishing disjointness; likewise the factorizer is trained and evaluated on the same 12M library.

The strongest quantitative results are obtained on a self-built synthetic library constructed via BRICS fragmentation of ZINC22 with explicitly no synthetic-feasibility guarantee (Section 3.1). This may not reflect real make-on-demand CSLs and could inflate factorizer reconstruction quality, undermining the headline benchmark.

The training objective adds isotropic noise to embeddings (Eq. 5) with the promise that its 'relevance... will be explained shortly,' but no explanation or justification appears; this is an unexplained and potentially load-bearing design choice for the linear-probe assumption.

The linear-probe surrogate parameterization (Eq. 3) imposes a strong linearity assumption on top of the factorization, yet there is no ablation on embedding dimension d, on the degree of linearity, or on how surrogate quality (docking-score R^2, which is known to be low and is worst for MET, Section 5.3.1) caps achievable recall.

Presentation problems: equations are garbled/duplicated (the Eq. 18 block contains repeated spurious 'subject to' lines), Figure 2 is difficult to parse, and Table 1's formatting is inconsistent, reducing confidence in the reported protocol.

The constraint-satisfaction result (Figure 2B) largely reflects that the search explicitly selects for the constraints, so it is weak evidence that the constraint surrogate is well modeled; the counter-screening/composite-objective results (Appendix A.11) are also only qualitatively reported.

The zero-shot Enamine REAL evaluation (Section 5.3.1) has no ground-truth top-k and is validated only against a 100,000-compound random background, so it provides distributional rather than retrieval-accuracy evidence.

strengths: Well-motivated and novel framing: the paper recasts virtual screening over combinatorial synthesis libraries (CSLs) as a top-k retrieval problem and exploits the CSL's combinatorial structure to factorize surrogate predictions into per-synthon associative contributions (Eqs. 14-17), enabling genuinely exhaustive evaluation rather than iterative sampling.

Strong, practical scalability: Table 1 shows APEX retrieving the top k=1M compounds from a 10B library in <30s and from a 70B Enamine REAL library in ~200s on a single Tesla T4 GPU, with order-of-magnitude speedups over the CPU implementation, especially as constraints are added.

Valuable amortization property: once the surrogate and factorizer are trained, changing objectives or constraint sets requires no retraining or oracle calls, a real advantage over the iterative/RL/generative approaches reviewed in Section 2.

A useful community benchmark: a 12M fully enumerated and exhaustively docked CSL across five diverse targets (PARP1, MET, DRD2, F10, ESR1) plus 28 physicochemical endpoints, enabling ground-truth top-j evaluation. Data leakage is carefully handled (surrogate trained on 1M, evaluated on 12M/10B).

The factorization is validated against the raw surrogate: Figure 10 shows factorized-surrogate recall closely tracks the unfactorized surrogate, and Appendix A.6/Figure 8 decomposes total NMSE into surrogate, factorizer, and cross terms, showing the cross term is negligible and giving actionable guidance for improvement.
Generality is demonstrated via a zero-shot application to the commercial Enamine REAL (9-2024) 70B library (Section 5.3.1), showing enrichment even without retraining.

Clear, readable presentation with informative figures (Fig. 1 workflow, Fig. 2 recall/constraint satisfaction) and adequate reproducibility (open benchmark, code repository, full architecture/training details in Appendix A.8).
weaknesses: Baseline comparison is thin. Only Thompson sampling (Klarich et al., 2024) is compared, only in the unconstrained setting, and only on the five largest reactions (~4M products). The related work discusses active learning (MolPal, MEMES, Deep Docking), RL, and generative methods, but none are benchmarked, weakening the claim of 'consistently strong performance compared to alternative methods.'

Novelty is incremental relative to Pedawi et al. (2022): the hierarchical Synthon/Rgroup/Reaction encoder stack and the additive factorization are largely inherited; the new contributions are the associative key/value maps and the top-k retrieval application. This is a reasonable engineering advance but not a fundamentally new method.

Recall is only moderate: top-100 recall is roughly 0.4-0.8 (Fig. 2A), meaning 20-60% of the true top compounds are missed. The paper does not analyze the practical consequences of these misses or characterize when the surrogate/factorizer fails.

No ablations on key design choices: embedding dimension (fixed at d=64), factorizer architecture, the noise-injection term in Eq. 5, and the size/diversity of factorizer training data are not systematically studied.

The constructed benchmark CSL is not synthetically feasible (BRICS recombination, acknowledged in Section 3.1), which may limit how representative it is of real make-on-demand CSLs, and its reactions may not match the statistics of vendor libraries.

Limitations are discussed only lightly; there is no dedicated limitations section and little discussion of failure modes (e.g., targets where enrichment drops, as noted for MET) or when the additive factorization assumption breaks down.
The phrasing 'exact retrieval of approximate top-k sets' is potentially confusing; retrieval is exact only with respect to the factorized surrogate, not the true objective.
